`createTrajectories()` returns a data frame and writes the same trajectory to
`Data/patientDataDiscrete.csv` or `Data/patientDataContinuous.csv` in the study
folder. Use column names rather than their positions when reading the result.

Printing the result shows patient and state counts followed by a short preview.
The object remains a data frame with every original column. Use:

```{r inspect-output, eval=FALSE}
trajectories                         # Compact preview
print(trajectories, n = 10)          # Show more rows
View(trajectories)                  # Browse all columns
as.data.frame(trajectories)         # Ordinary data-frame display
```

The preview distinguishes clinical states from boundary and unresolved rows.
It does not alter the trajectory data or the saved CSV.

## Columns

| Column | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `subject_id` | The original patient identifier. Internal batching IDs are not exported. |
| `state_label` | The selected clinical label, or `START`, `EXIT` or `OUT OF COHORT`. |
| `state_start_date` | First date of the selected interval or discrete cycle. |
| `state_end_date` | Last date of that interval or cycle, including this date. |
| `time_in_cohort` | Years from trajectory start to this row's start, calculated as elapsed days divided by 365.25. |
| `seq_ordinal` | Consecutive occurrence number of the same label in that patient's output rows. It resets when the label changes. It is not a cycle number. |
| `state_id` | An identifier assigned to the label within the run. It is not a clinical concept ID or a cross-database key. |
| `age` | Age in years at this row's start, when a CDM demographic join is used. Otherwise `NA`. |
| `gender_concept_id` | The CDM person's recorded gender concept ID, when joined. Otherwise `NA`. |
| `state_key` | Present only for merged studies. Identifies the original members of a state across runs with the same labels. |

Dates are `Date` values in the returned R object and date strings in CSV.
`state_id` may be character or numeric depending on the trajectory format.
Treat it as an identifier, not as a quantity. For unmerged output, inspect its
mapping with `unique(trajectories[c("state_id", "state_label")])`.

When reading a CSV, preserve patient identifiers as text:

```{r read-csv, eval=FALSE}
trajectories <- read.csv(
  "MyStudy/Data/patientDataDiscrete.csv",
  colClasses = "character",
  na.strings = NULL
)
trajectories$state_start_date <- as.Date(trajectories$state_start_date)
trajectories$state_end_date <- as.Date(trajectories$state_end_date)
for (column in c("time_in_cohort", "seq_ordinal", "age", "gender_concept_id")) {
  trajectories[[column]] <- type.convert(trajectories[[column]], as.is = TRUE)
}
```

This keeps leading zeros, long identifiers and literal labels such as `"NA"`.
Only the known numeric columns are converted. For input
already held in R, use character or `integer64` values for large identifiers.
The package cannot recover digits already rounded by numeric storage.

## Observation boundaries and unresolved cycles

The first target-cohort interval supplies the trajectory's start and end.
An absorbing state can stop the trajectory earlier. With
`outOfCohortAllowed = TRUE`, retained state records can extend its end, but not
move its start earlier. The analyst is responsible for supplying valid
observation bounds.

`START` marks the first date. `EXIT` marks the day after the retained follow-up
endpoint. For discrete output, that is the end of the final cycle. Both markers
have identical start and end dates. They do
not contribute observed days and should not be counted as clinical states
when estimating time spent in care.

`OUT OF COHORT` has a different meaning. It is a discrete cycle for which no
state was selected. The cycle is still within the supplied observation period.
Deleting such rows can make separated states look like adjacent observations.
Choose how an analysis handles these gaps before estimating transitions.

## Discrete dates are cycle dates

With `cycleLength = 7`, a cycle beginning January 1 ends January 7. The next
begins January 8. If observation ends January 10, that final cycle contains
three observed days. For non-marker rows, duration is
`as.integer(state_end_date - state_start_date) + 1`.

One label represents the whole cycle according to the configured selection
rule. Its start date is not necessarily the date that the selected event
occurred. A selected death state stops generation after its cycle. The cycle
is shortened to the actual death date only if the supplied trajectory boundary
also ends there.

Separate death states can preserve whether a complication had occurred before
death, if the analyst defines them that way. They do not preserve the exact
within-week complication date. See the [weekly example](a04_example.html).

## Continuous dates are interval dates

Continuous output keeps the selected interval endpoints, bounded by the target
interval and absorbing-state rules. It does not invent state coverage in a gap
or shift simultaneous records onto different days. Priority selection can
split intervals. First and Overlap selection can retain overlapping intervals.

Two rows can therefore share a start date or cover some of the same days.
A downstream model that needs one state at every instant must handle that
explicitly. Summing overlapping interval lengths will overcount patient-time.

## State membership

For merged studies, `study$stateDictionary` and `Data/stateDictionary.rds`
describe each original or combined state:

| Field | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `state_key` | Stable key built from the original member labels. |
| `label` | Display label used in the trajectory. |
| `members` | List of original state labels. |
| `absorbing` | Whether selecting this state ends the trajectory. |
| `allowedTransitions` | List of permitted destination keys. |
| `state_id` | Run-local ID, added during generation. |

Use `members` to inspect a combination. Do not split its display label or key.
The dictionary does not include boundary or unresolved-gap markers. Unmerged
studies do not produce this dictionary.

## Files to keep

| File | Purpose |
|:--|:--|
| `Settings/analysisSettings.rds` | Completed import and generation rules. For CDM studies it also contains the cohort JSON definitions used during import. |
| `Data/patientDataDiscrete.csv` or `Data/patientDataContinuous.csv` | Patient trajectories. |
| `Data/importedDataCleaned.csv` | Intervals used as input to trajectory generation. The filename is independent of the cohort-definition path. |
| `Data/sourceIntervals.rds` | Merged studies only. Cleaned intervals before overlapping states were combined. |
| `Data/stateDictionary.rds` | Merged studies only. Membership and resolved state rules. |

The interval files have already been cleaned. Observation limits and mandatory
state requirements have been applied, and overlapping records of the same
state have been combined. They are not a copy of every original database row.
In merged studies, use `sourceIntervals.rds` to inspect the original state
labels before composition.

The version-5 settings file stores `import` and `generation` separately because
some choices can be supplied at generation time. For example, the cycle length
is under `settings$generation$cycleLength`. Version 4 settings still load, with
the old `lengthOfStay` field translated to `cycleLength`. Clinical rules remain
the analyst's responsibility even though their execution settings are saved.

When sharing a study, copy `Settings`, not `Data`. The settings file contains no
patient records or database connection. It does include study-specific cohort
definitions, which should be reviewed before sharing.

## Handing the result to an analysis package

The returned data frame has a `trajectory_definition` attribute with its
format version, trajectory type, cycle length, ordered clinical labels and
absorbing labels. It records the rules actually used for generation, including
merged-state overrides and configured states absent from this dataset. It
contains no copy of the patient rows or study environment.

TMA reads these definitions when you pass the output directly:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
histories <- TrajectoryMarkovAnalysis::prepareTrajectories(trajectories)
transitions <- TrajectoryMarkovAnalysis::estimateTransitions(histories)
```

RDS saves and ordinary data-frame row subsets retain the definitions. A CSV
contains only the rows. After reading a CSV, supply the cycle length, state
labels and absorbing states to TMA explicitly. Do not infer them from label
spelling or numeric IDs. A transformation that changes the state meanings or
cycle lengths also needs a new definition. TMA rejects settings that conflict
with the attached definition.

For merged-state membership, keep the separate state dictionary. The compact
handoff supplies resolved labels and absorbing status, not the full selection
or transition rules.

Cohort2Trajectory constructs histories. It does not estimate transition
probabilities, survival effects, costs or cost-effectiveness. Check that the
downstream package accepts the current column names and identifiers, treats
observation end separately from a clinical outcome, and handles shortened
cycles as intended. Exact event-time analyses also need the relevant state
intervals rather than dates inferred from weekly labels.
